about: Crock’s notes: short, plain-language overviews of well-known RFCs — why each was written, and where it made a difference. Drafted with AI assistance for this prototype; an editor should review each one before it is used anywhere real.

1.why: In 1969 a handful of graduate students were working out how the first ARPANET computers should talk to each other. Steve Crocker wrote their ideas up as a modest “request for comments” — and the name stuck.
1.where: Every RFC since, including the ones that run today’s internet, carries on the open, anyone-can-comment habit this memo started.

768.why: Not everything needs TCP’s careful, guaranteed delivery. UDP is the lightweight option: send a packet and move on, with almost no overhead.
768.where: DNS lookups, video calls, online games and QUIC all ride on UDP, because speed matters more to them than perfection.

791.why: Networks built by different people needed one shared way to address and forward packets. IP is that common language: every packet gets a from and a to, and routers pass it along.
791.where: This is IPv4 — the 192.168.1.1-style addresses that still carry much of the internet’s traffic more than forty years on.

792.why: When something goes wrong in the network — a host can’t be reached, a packet wanders too long — routers need a way to say so. ICMP is IP’s little messaging system for errors and checks.
792.where: Every time someone runs ping or traceroute, they’re sending ICMP messages.

793.why: IP delivers packets but promises nothing. TCP adds the promises: data arrives complete, in order, and at a pace the network can handle.
793.where: For four decades it carried the web, email and file transfers. In 2022 it was brought together with its many updates in RFC 9293.

826.why: On a local network, knowing a machine’s IP address isn’t enough — you need its hardware address to deliver anything. ARP asks the network “who has this address?” and remembers the answer.
826.where: Every device on a home or office network uses it, quietly, all the time.

1034.why: Early on, every computer’s name lived in one shared file that had to be copied around by hand. DNS replaced it with a directory spread across many servers, which anyone can look names up in.
1034.where: Every time you type a web address, DNS turns the name into an IP address — usually in a few milliseconds.

1035.why: The companion to RFC 1034: where that one explains the ideas, this one pins down the actual messages and record formats that DNS servers exchange.
1035.where: Record types you still see today — A, MX, TXT — and the way DNS messages are packed, come from here.

1122.why: By the late 1980s, different systems disagreed on the fine print. This RFC set out what every internet-connected computer must, should and may do.
1122.where: It’s still the reference behind how operating systems handle IP, TCP and UDP.

1149.why: An April Fools’ joke: a perfectly deadpan specification for sending internet packets by carrier pigeon.
1149.where: A reminder that the RFC series has a sense of humour — and in 2001 a group in Bergen, Norway actually tried it, pigeons and all.

1321.why: MD5 turns any data into a short fingerprint, so you can check that a file hasn’t changed.
1321.where: It became hugely popular, then researchers broke it. Today it’s fine for spotting accidental damage, but it must not be trusted for security.

1918.why: IPv4 addresses were running short, and most computers inside companies didn’t need to be reachable from outside. This RFC set aside ranges that anyone can use privately.
1918.where: It’s why your home network uses 192.168.x.x or 10.x.x.x addresses behind your router.

1945.why: The web was already booming when this was written. It recorded how browsers and servers were actually talking, so everyone could agree on the basics.
1945.where: Requests, headers and status codes like 404 were written down here, and HTTP still uses them.

1958.why: Written to capture what had made the internet work so far: keep the network simple and put the cleverness at the edges — the “end-to-end” idea.
1958.where: Those principles still come up whenever people argue about how a new protocol should be designed.

2026.why: Someone had to write down how an idea becomes an internet standard. This RFC describes the path: drafts, review, then the standards track.
2026.where: It’s the rulebook behind the statuses you see on every RFC here — Proposed Standard, Internet Standard, Best Current Practice.

2045.why: Early email could only carry plain English text. MIME added a way to label and package everything else: other languages, pictures, attachments.
2045.where: Every email attachment uses it, and its content types — text/html, image/png — became the web’s way of labelling files too.

2119.why: Specifications used “must” and “should” loosely, which led to arguments about what was really required. This one-page RFC pinned down exactly what they mean.
2119.where: Nearly every RFC written since cites it — it’s where the capital-letter MUST and SHOULD across the series come from.

2131.why: Setting an IP address by hand on every computer doesn’t scale. DHCP lets a device join a network and be handed an address and settings automatically.
2131.where: It’s what happens every time your phone or laptop connects to Wi-Fi.

2324.why: Another April Fools’ RFC: a protocol for controlling, monitoring and diagnosing coffee pots over the internet.
2324.where: It gave the web the famous “418 I’m a teapot” error, which still turns up — affectionately — in real software.

2616.why: The web quickly outgrew HTTP/1.0. HTTP/1.1 added reusing connections, hosting many sites on one server, and much better caching.
2616.where: For fifteen years it was the web’s rulebook. It has since been split up and rewritten; today’s version lives in RFCs 9110–9112.

2818.why: Secure websites were already common, but how HTTP should run inside an encrypted connection had never been written down. This short RFC did — it’s the “https” in web addresses.
2818.where: Its rules, like checking that a certificate matches the site’s name, were folded into HTTP Semantics (RFC 9110) in 2022.

3261.why: Calls over the internet need a way to find someone, ring them and agree on how to talk. SIP handles that calling part — a bit like HTTP, but for phone calls.
3261.where: It sits behind most internet phone systems: office desk phones, many calling apps and phone carriers’ own networks.

3339.why: Dates were written a dozen different ways, which caused endless mix-ups. This RFC picked one clear format: 2002-07-15T12:00:00Z.
3339.where: You’ll find it in logs, APIs and JSON data all over the web.

3550.why: Live audio and video need to arrive in order and on time, not just eventually. RTP adds timestamps and sequence numbers so the other end can play media smoothly.
3550.where: Nearly every voice and video call — from desk phones to browser video chats — carries its sound and pictures over RTP.

3629.why: Computers had hundreds of incompatible ways to store text in different languages. UTF-8 can encode every character in Unicode while staying compatible with plain ASCII.
3629.where: It’s now the encoding of almost every web page, email and piece of source code.

3986.why: Web addresses had grown plenty of edge cases. This RFC defines exactly how an address is built — scheme, host, path, query, fragment — and how to read one.
3986.where: Every link you click, and every browser and server that makes sense of it, follows these rules.

4122.why: Programs often need an ID that’s unique without asking any central authority. UUIDs are 128-bit IDs that anyone can generate, with practically no chance of a clash.
4122.where: They’re everywhere in software — database keys, file formats, device IDs. In 2024 RFC 9562 replaced this spec and added time-ordered versions.

4253.why: Remote logins used to send passwords across the network in the clear. SSH wraps the whole session in encryption and checks that you’re talking to the right server.
4253.where: It’s how developers and administrators log into servers — and how many of them push code with git.

4271.why: The internet is tens of thousands of separately run networks. BGP is how they tell each other which addresses they can reach, so traffic can find its way across.
4271.where: It’s the glue between internet providers — and when a BGP announcement goes wrong, large parts of the internet can briefly vanish.

4648.why: Plenty of systems can only carry plain text safely. Base64 turns any data into letters and digits, and this RFC pins down exactly how.
4648.where: It shows up in email attachments, data: URLs, web tokens and countless APIs.

4961.why: Voice and video calls often failed to cross home routers and firewalls, because devices sent media from one port and listened on another. This RFC named the simple fix: send and receive on the same port.
4961.where: Most internet phones and calling apps now work this way, which makes calls far more likely to get through NATs and firewalls.

5246.why: TLS is the lock on secure connections. Version 1.2 modernised its cryptography and became the long-running workhorse of HTTPS.
5246.where: For about a decade it secured most of the web. TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446) replaced it in 2018, but 1.2 is still widely supported.

5280.why: Certificates prove a website is who it says it is, but the underlying X.509 standard left too many options open. This RFC narrowed it down to what the internet actually uses.
5280.where: Every padlock in your browser rests on certificates checked by these rules.

5321.why: Email needs a way to hand messages from server to server until they reach the right inbox. SMTP is that relay; this is its current version, going back to RFC 821 in 1982.
5321.where: Almost every email sent today travels between servers over SMTP.

5322.why: An email isn’t just text: it has a From, a To, a Subject and a Date. This RFC defines how those headers and the message body are laid out, going back to RFC 822 in 1982.
5322.where: Every email in every inbox follows this format, whichever app you use.

5646.why: Software needs a way to say which language — and which variety of it — some text is in. This RFC defines short tags like en-GB, pt-BR and zh-Hant.
5646.where: Your browser sends them to websites so pages come back in your language, and apps use them for spelling and translations.

5905.why: Computer clocks drift, and a network whose clocks disagree breaks in subtle ways. NTP lets machines ask trusted time servers and set themselves accurately.
5905.where: Your phone and laptop keep the right time thanks to it — and so do the servers checking your logins and certificates.

6265.why: HTTP forgets you between page loads. Cookies let a site remember small things — that you’re signed in, what’s in your basket — and this RFC finally described how they really work.
6265.where: Every login and shopping basket on the web relies on cookies — and so, less happily, does a lot of tracking.

6376.why: Anyone can type any address into an email’s From line. DKIM lets the sending domain sign its messages, so receivers can check they really came from there and weren’t changed.
6376.where: Big mail providers check it on almost every message; it’s one of the main defences against spoofed email and phishing.

6455.why: Web pages could only get fresh data by asking the server again and again. WebSocket opens a lasting two-way channel, so the server can send updates the moment they happen.
6455.where: Live chat, collaborative editors, trading screens and multiplayer browser games all use it.

6749.why: Apps used to ask for your actual password to reach your data elsewhere. OAuth lets you grant limited access with a token instead, without ever handing over the password.
6749.where: “Sign in with…” buttons and most app-to-app connections are built on it.

7208.why: Spammers can send mail pretending to be from any domain. SPF lets a domain publish a list of the servers allowed to send its email.
7208.where: Mail providers check it on incoming messages — together with DKIM and DMARC — to catch forgeries.

7231.why: RFC 2616 had grown sprawling and sometimes contradictory, so the HTTP working group split it into six clearer documents. This one covers what requests and responses mean.
7231.where: It guided HTTP for eight years before being folded into RFC 9110 in 2022.

7234.why: Part of the 2014 rewrite of HTTP/1.1, this RFC explains when a stored copy of a response can be reused, and when it has to be checked again.
7234.where: Its rules shaped browser and CDN caching until RFC 9111 replaced it in 2022.

7282.why: The IETF decides by “rough consensus” — sometimes by humming rather than voting. This RFC explains what that really means, and why a simple majority isn’t enough.
7282.where: It’s one of the clearest windows into how the people behind these documents actually make decisions.

7489.why: SPF and DKIM can check an email, but a domain had no way to say what should happen when those checks fail. DMARC lets it publish a policy — such as “reject fakes” — and get reports back.
7489.where: Large mail providers now expect it from anyone sending email in bulk; it’s a big reason spoofed bank emails get caught.

7519.why: Web services needed a compact, signed way to pass claims like “this user is Alice” between systems. A JWT is a small JSON token that can be checked without calling home.
7519.where: They carry sign-ins and permissions in a huge number of web and mobile apps, often alongside OAuth.

7540.why: Pages had grown to hundreds of files, and HTTP/1.1 fetched them clumsily. HTTP/2 sends many requests at once over a single connection, in a compact binary form.
7540.where: It made the web noticeably faster and quickly became the default in browsers. Its updated version is RFC 9113.

8174.why: People weren’t sure whether a lowercase “must” carried the same force as MUST. This short update settles it: only the capitalised words are the special ones.
8174.where: Most RFCs now cite it right next to RFC 2119; together they make up BCP 14.

8200.why: IPv4’s roughly four billion addresses were never going to be enough. IPv6 has so many that every device can have its own, with room to spare.
8200.where: A large and growing share of traffic — especially on mobile networks — now travels over IPv6.

8259.why: JSON grew out of JavaScript as a simple way to write data as text. This RFC nails down the exact rules, so every system reads it the same way.
8259.where: It’s the everyday format of web APIs — when an app talks to a server, it’s usually swapping JSON.

8446.why: TLS 1.2 had collected weak options and took extra round trips to connect. Version 1.3 removed the risky parts and made secure connections faster to set up.
8446.where: Most HTTPS connections from modern browsers now use it — it’s the padlock, updated.

8555.why: Getting a certificate for HTTPS used to be slow, manual and often paid for. ACME lets a server prove it controls a domain and get a certificate automatically.
8555.where: It’s the protocol behind Let’s Encrypt, which helped make HTTPS the normal way to browse.

8890.why: When the interests of companies, governments and people clash, whose side should internet standards take? This RFC answers plainly: the people using the internet.
8890.where: It’s become a touchstone in IETF debates about privacy, and about who a protocol really serves.

9000.why: TCP is hard to change and slow to start, especially on mobile. QUIC rebuilds reliable, encrypted transport on top of UDP, with quicker connections that survive switching networks.
9000.where: It carries HTTP/3, so a large share of traffic from big websites and apps now runs over it.

9110.why: HTTP now comes in three versions — 1.1, 2 and 3 — that all mean the same things: methods, status codes, headers. This RFC gathers that shared meaning in one place.
9110.where: It’s the core definition of how the web talks today; every browser, server and web API builds on it.

9111.why: Reusing a saved copy of a response saves time and data — as long as you know it’s still good. This RFC sets out those rules for every version of HTTP.
9111.where: Browsers, CDNs and proxies use it to decide what they can serve without asking the original site again.

9112.why: With HTTP’s meaning moved into RFC 9110, this document covers only how HTTP/1.1 messages are written out on the wire.
9112.where: HTTP/1.1 is still everywhere — in APIs, in small devices, and as the fallback when newer versions aren’t available.

9113.why: An update of HTTP/2 (RFC 7540) that lines it up with the new HTTP Semantics and drops a prioritisation scheme that never worked well in practice.
9113.where: Browsers and servers use it across a huge share of the web, alongside HTTP/3.

9114.why: HTTP/3 carries the same HTTP over QUIC instead of TCP, so one lost packet no longer holds up everything else, and connections start faster.
9114.where: Big websites and browsers already use it widely — it helps most on phones and patchy connections.

9293.why: RFC 793 had gathered forty years of fixes, scattered across many documents. This RFC brings them together into one up-to-date description of TCP.
9293.where: It’s the version anyone building TCP should read today: the same protocol, finally all in one place.

9562.why: An update to the classic UUID specification (RFC 4122) that adds new versions — including ones ordered by time, which work much better as database keys.
9562.where: Libraries and databases are adopting its time-ordered UUIDv7.
